Direct multi-step forecasts from local projections

Source: R/lp-forecast.R
lp_forecast.Rd

For each horizon \(h=1,\dots,H\) regresses \(y_{t+h}\) on \(x_t=(1,y_t',\dots,y_{t-p+1}')'\) and forecasts \(\hat y_{T+h}=x_T'\hat B_h\). The forecast standard error is \(\hat\sigma_h\sqrt{1+x_T'(X_h'X_h)^{-1}x_T}\) (the direct-regression residual has an MA(h-1) structure but its unconditional variance is what matters for the forecast error).

Usage

lp_forecast(Y, horizon = 8L, lags = 4L, level = c(0.68, 0.9))

Arguments

Y

data frame / tibble / matrix (T x K); non-numeric columns are dropped.

horizon

maximum forecast horizon.

lags

number of lags \(p\).

level

confidence levels for the bands.

Value

an lp_forecast object: $mean, $se (H x K), $bands (H x K x 2*length(level)). tidy() returns a tibble.

Details

Economic intuition. Iterated (VAR) forecasts are efficient if the VAR is correctly specified but compound any misspecification with the horizon; direct forecasts estimate each horizon's conditional mean separately, which is robust to misspecification but noisier (Marcellino, Stock & Watson 2006). Prefer direct forecasts at long horizons with long samples and a possibly nonlinear/mis-specified dynamics, iterated forecasts when the sample is short. At \(h=1\) the two coincide exactly. Pitfall: forecasts at different horizons are not constrained to be consistent with each other and can be jagged.

See also

Other local projections: autoplot.lpm(), compare_lp_var(), lp(), lp_joint(), lp_panel(), lp_smooth(), lp_state(), lp_supt(), tidy.lpm()

Examples

lp_forecast(yraw, horizon = 4, lags = 2)
#> <lp_forecast> direct forecasts, horizons 1..4
#>     infl  unemp   rate
#> 1 2.7209 4.9214 4.6197
#> 2 2.6601 5.0377 4.4461
#> 3 2.6606 5.2093 4.2187
#> 4 2.7711 5.3189 4.2035
